Esthetic appeal and \nsocial presence, in turn, positively predicted both purchase intention and brand \ntrust. Independent of these cognitive pathways, AI disclosure labels carried a \npositive direct effect on purchase intention (b = 0.308, p = 0.010) that was not \nmoderated by product type, while showing no significant direct effect on brand \ntrust. Because this direct effect ran opposite in sign to the negative indirect path-\nways through esthetic appeal and social presence, the overall (total) effect of AI \nlabels appeared weak or even negative in raw form, a pattern consistent with \ninconsistent mediation (suppression).\nDiscussion: These findings refine the traditional source-information consistency \naccount of algorithm aversion and highlight the need for context-sensitive, plat-\nform-level governance of AI-generated product imagery in e-commerce.\nKEYWORDS\nAI disclosure, algorithm aversion, consumer behavior, context-sensitive AI governance, \nproduct type"}, {"pdf_page": 2, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 02 frontiersin.org\n1 Introduction\n1.1 AI-generated product imagery in \nE-commerce\nAt its core, this study is about a labeling dynamic: how does dis-\nclosing something about the source of a product image change a shop-\nper’s response, relative to disclosing nothing at all? Explicit source \ndisclosure is not new to e-commerce interfaces, sellers already label \nproducts as handmade, imported, or certified, and the psychological \nlogic of such labels has long been studied as a general phenomenon of \nsource disclosure. What is new, and what motivates the present study, \nis that AI-generated content has recently become one of the most con-\nsequential kinds of content a disclosure label can reveal. We therefore \ntreat AI-generated versus human-generated as two instances of label \ncontent, compared against a shared no-label baseline, and ask how the \npresence of a label, and what that label discloses, shapes shopper \nresponses.\nGenerative artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming \nhow digital product imagery is produced for online retail. AI models \ncan now create highly realistic product images on demand, eliminat-\ning traditional photography costs and production barriers (Dar and \nGul, 2025; Hartmann et al., 2024). This shift is especially visible on \nlarge e-commerce platforms, where sellers increasingly rely on \nAI-generated visuals for product images, the kind a shopper sees while \nbrowsing a listing or reviewing a product before purchase. On plat-\nforms such as Taobao, AI-generated product images have moved from \na novelty to a routine production tool used across many product cat-\negories, from small electronics to cosmetics and fragrance. However, \nwhether shoppers adapt comfortably to this shift remains an open \nquestion, and early evidence suggests they may not do so uniformly.\nGlobal regulators have responded to these developments. Driven \nby concerns about deepfakes and synthetic media, policymakers have \nshifted from voluntary guidelines to enforceable legal requirements. \nFor example, regulations such as the EU’s Artificial Intelligence Act \nand China’s Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI \nServices now require explicit disclosure of AI-generated content \n(Jobin et al., 2019 ; Madiega, 2024 ). In practice, this means that \n“ AI-generated” labels are becoming a standard element of e-commerce \ninterface design, appearing alongside product images on listing and \ndetail pages in much the same way that other source cues (seller \nbadges, certification marks) already do. Unlike most interface cues, \nhowever, an AI-generated label indicates that the visual content was \nnot produced by a human photographer, representing a type of infor-\nmation of a qualitatively different nature that shoppers have little prior \nexperience evaluating (Schilke and Reimann, 2025). AI disclosure is \ntherefore a particularly consequential, currently unfolding instance of \nthe general labeling dynamic introduced above: it lets us ask not only \nwhether a label is present, but whether what the label discloses, a \nmachine origin, changes shopper responses differently than other \nlabel content would.\nThis is at once a design challenge and a regulatory one. Mandatory \ndisclosure labels introduce a new cognitive variable into the product \npage that platform designers cannot ignore. From a human–computer \ninteraction perspective, AI disclosure labels on e-commerce product \npages are not merely regulatory notices; they function as interface-\nlevel source cues that reshape how shoppers attribute agency, authen-\nticity, social presence, and risk to the product images in front of them. \nRather than treating disclosure only as a persuasion problem, we \nconceptualize it as a design variable embedded in human–\nAI-mediated commerce, with implications for transparency design, \nplatform trust, and context-sensitive AI governance.\nExisting research is divided: some work suggests algorithmic dis-\nclosure labels undermine user trust (Oomen et al., 2024), while other \nwork suggests they can increase credibility. This divergence cannot be \nexplained by disclosure condition alone. Prior research shows that \nuser responses to AI vary across utilitarian and hedonic product \ndomains, yet less is known about how AI disclosure labels operate as \ninterface-level source cues specifically within e-commerce product \npages, or which cognitive responses they activate. The gap addressed \nin this study is not the absence of product-context research, but the \nlimited understanding of how AI disclosure cues on e-commerce \nproduct pages shape shoppers’ interpretation of synthetic visual con-\ntent through specific, testable cognitive pathways.\n1.2 Research objectives\nReturning to the labeling dynamic introduced in Section 1.1, and \nbuilding on prior research on algorithm aversion and utilitarian–\nhedonic differences in AI evaluation, this study focuses on a specific \ne-commerce interface problem: how mandatory source disclosure \nlabels on product images function as interface cues and shape pur-\nchase-relevant judgments, using AI-generated content as the focal case \nand human-generated content as a second, comparison case of what \na label can disclose. Rather than asking only whether shoppers prefer \nor reject AI-generated imagery, we examine how disclosure labels, and \nthe content they disclose, reshape shoppers’ cognitive interpretation \nof that imagery and how these interpretations connect to brand trust \nand purchase intention.\nThis study pursues three objectives. First, we examine how source \ndisclosure labels, as interface-level transparency cues on e-commerce \nproduct pages, shape shoppers’ evaluative and behavioral responses \nrelative to a no-label baseline, distinguishing between the general \npresence of a label and the specific content it discloses by comparing \nAI-generated and human-generated label conditions. Second, we \nidentify the cognitive mechanisms through which AI-generated label \ncontent in particular operates, focusing on three mediating variables \nretained as the core analytic focus of this study: perceived authenticity, \nesthetic appeal, and social presence. (Two further constructs, per -\nceived risk and the uncanny valley effect, were also measured and \ntested; because neither showed a reliable first-stage or second-stage \neffect in any product context, neither is carried through the detailed \nresults reported below; a brief summary of their null pattern is given \nin Section 5.4, consistent with the goal of presenting a focused, well-\npowered account of the pathways that matter most.) These three \nretained variables are conceptualized as parallel cognitive responses \nrather than sequential stages in a single causal chain: source-related \njudgment (authenticity), visual evaluation (esthetic appeal), and per-\nceived human presence (social presence). Third, we test whether prod-\nuct context (utilitarian vs. hedonic) moderates the first-stage effect of \nAI disclosure on each of these three pathways, using a conditional \nprocess (moderated-mediation) framework with bootstrapped confi-\ndence intervals, thereby determining the boundary conditions under \nwhich AI disclosure labels function differently across product \ncategories.\nWe employed a 3 × 2 between-subjects experimental design, \nmanipulating disclosure condition and product type. By holding all \nother interface elements of the simulated product page constant, we "}, {"pdf_page": 3, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 03 frontiersin.org\nisolate the cognitive effects of the disclosure cue itself. The findings \naim to inform the design of AI disclosure systems on e-commerce \nplatforms and how shoppers process source information about \nAI-generated product imagery.\n2 Literature review\n2.1 AI disclosure as an interface cue in \nE-commerce\nIn human–computer interaction research, interface cues are \ndesign elements that carry information beyond their surface appear-\nance, shaping how users understand and respond to a system \n(Norman, 2004). A disclosure label is one such cue: whatever it dis-\ncloses, its presence versus absence changes what a shopper knows \nabout the image in front of them. On e-commerce product pages, \nthese labels function as source cues, indicating who, or what, pro -\nduced the image a shopper is evaluating. Regarding AI disclosure \nspecifically, the literature documents two competing patterns.\nAlgorithm aversion refers to the tendency for people to discount \nor reject AI-generated outputs even when their quality is objectively \ncomparable to human-generated outputs. Castelo et al. (2019) suggest \nthis reaction is task-specific, more likely when the task involves sub-\njective judgment, of the kind involved in evaluating a product photo. \nMillet et al. (2023)  attribute this to anthropocentric bias: negative \nreactions to AI signals reflect assumptions about the meaning of the \noutput, not simply an assessment of its quality.\nNot all users react this way. Logg et al. (2019) show that in some \nsituations, people trust an algorithm’s output more than human judg-\nment, especially when objectivity and accuracy are valued, a phenom-\nenon they term “algorithmic appreciation. ” Oomen et al. (2024)  \nfurther show that algorithmic appreciation or aversion largely depends \non the specific evaluative context, which for e-commerce product \nimagery plausibly includes both the product category being shown \nand the shopping task the image supports.\n2.2 Cognitive pathways between disclosure \nand shopper response\nThis study treats three mediating variables, perceived authenticity, \nesthetic appeal, and social presence, as parallel cognitive pathways \nactivated by AI disclosure labels on e-commerce product pages. They \nare not proposed as a sequential process. Perceived authenticity \nreflects a shopper’s attribution of human creative intent and genuine-\nness behind a product image; esthetic appeal reflects visual fluency \nand pleasure in viewing the image; and social presence reflects the \nperceived warmth and human presence conveyed by the product page.\nShoppers typically expect product images to reflect genuine \nhuman creative effort, and this expectation forms the basis of their \nperception of image authenticity (MacInnis and Price, 1987). When a \nlabel indicates that an image originated from a machine, even if the \nimage is visually convincing, it undermines this expectation at a cog-\nnitive level; disclosure reshapes shoppers’ interpretation of the image’s \norigin and dispels the default assumption of a human creator behind \nit (Jago, 2017).\nEsthetic appeal reflects the visual pleasure evoked by a product \nimage during processing (Tractinsky et al., 2000). Processing fluency \ntheory predicts that well-structured stimuli are processed more easily, \ngenerating positive affect that is attributed to the content itself (Reber \net al., 2004). AI-generated images can achieve a high degree of visual \npolish (Cetinic and She, 2022), and in some cases AI labels may rein-\nforce rather than weaken esthetic evaluations by signaling technical \nquality (Verganti et al., 2020).\nSocial presence reflects the warmth and psychological “co-pres-\nence” a shopper experiences when viewing a product page (Short et \nal., 1976; Hassanein and Head, 2007). When shoppers learn that a \nproduct image is AI-generated, they may perceive a lack of genuine \nemotional investment from a human creator. Sundar (2020) links this \nsense of indifference to “machine heuristics, ” the intuitive belief that \nalgorithms inherently lack empathy; Mende et al. (2019) document a \nsimilar anthropomorphic-deprivation effect in service-robot \ninteractions.\nTwo additional constructs, perceived risk and the uncanny valley \neffect, were measured using the same procedures as the three retained \npathways above, motivated by the same broad theoretical logic (that \nAI disclosure could heighten uncertainty about product performance, \nand that machine origin could produce a sense of artificiality even for \nnon-humanoid product images). Neither showed a reliable effect in \nthis study, and this null pattern is discussed further in Section 6.\n2.3 The moderating effect of product \ncontext\nHuman–computer interaction research has consistently shown \nthat the cognitive effect of an interface cue depends on the user’s task \ngoals and the evaluative orientation those goals activate ( Norman, \n2004). Information-source-consistency theory formalizes this: when \nthe source of interface content matches a user’s situational expecta-\ntions, processing is smoother ( Lee and Aaker, 2004 ); a mismatch \nrequires additional cognitive effort to resolve ( Kim and \nDuhachek, 2020).\nUtilitarian and hedonic product contexts activate different pro-\ncessing orientations (Dhar and Wertenbroch, 2000). In utilitarian \ne-commerce categories such as small electronics, AI disclosure may \ncreate competing expectations: it may signal computational precision, \nwhich fits expectations for functional products, but utilitarian prod-\nucts also raise stronger concerns about reliability and real-world per-\nformance, so AI disclosure may trigger caution if shoppers suspect \nthe product image is overly optimized. In hedonic categories such as \nfragrance, shoppers seek emotional resonance and human creative \nexpression, and an AI label may conflict with these expectations \n(Batra and Ahtola, 1991; Longoni and Cian, 2022). Longoni and Cian \n(2022) found that the same AI system is evaluated more favorably in \npractical domains than in hedonic domains, a pattern they term the \n“word-of-machine effect. ”\nA concurrent study by Shi and Jiang (2026) proposes a related but \ndistinct account of AI disclosure effects in advertising, modeling a \ntrade-off between two competing pathways, perceived novelty and \nperceived authenticity, moderated by a shopper’s regulatory focus, \nand also examining product type as a second-stage moderator of this \ntrade-off. The present study differs in structure and scope: rather than \nmodeling a single novelty–authenticity trade-off, we test product type \nas a first-stage moderator of AI disclosure’s effect across three parallel \ncognitive pathways (authenticity, esthetic appeal, social presence) \nspecifically within an e-commerce product-page context, using a \nbootstrapped conditional process framework. These two studies can "}, {"pdf_page": 4, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 04 frontiersin.org\nbe read as complementary accounts of the same underlying phenom-\nenon, approached from different theoretical entry points and inter-\nface contexts (general advertising versus e-commerce product pages).\n2.4 Shopper trust and behavioral \nengagement\nThis study uses two constructs to operationalize behavioral \noutcomes. Brand trust is a form of shopper–platform trust, reflect -\ning confidence in the competence, integrity, and non-deceptive \nintent of the product page’s source ( Mayer et al., 1995 ); even indi -\nrect signals of possible manipulation can weaken this trust \n(Ahluwalia et al., 2000 ). Purchase intention reflects a shopper’s \nwillingness to act on the product page in front of them ( Dodds et \nal., 1991 ); such intentions are sensitive to source and quality cues, \nmaking purchase intention an appropriate behavioral endpoint for \ntesting disclosure effects.\n2.5 A dual-track mechanism of AI \ndisclosure\nAI disclosure labels may influence shoppers through two simul-\ntaneous tracks. The first is a cognitive-penalty pathway: disclosing \nthat a product image is AI-generated may weaken perceived authen-\nticity, reduce social presence, or reduce esthetic appeal, changing how \nshoppers interpret the source and agency behind the image. The \nsecond is a transparency or novelty-signal pathway: disclosure may \nindependently signal openness and honesty, or convey a sense of \ntechnological currency, increasing trust or purchase interest through \na channel that is separate from, and can run in the opposite direction \nto, the cognitive-penalty pathway. As detailed in Section 5, the pres-\nent data are consistent with both tracks operating simultaneously and \nwith partially offsetting signs, a pattern statistically identifiable as \ninconsistent mediation (suppression) once both the indirect and \ndirect effects are estimated within the same model.\n3 Hypotheses\nThe design manipulates disclosure condition at three levels \n(AI-generated label, human-generated label, no label), all esti -\nmated against the same no-label baseline, which serves as the \nsingle reference/control condition throughout. The hypotheses \nbelow treat both label types as manipulated conditions rather than \ntreating one as a passive comparison arm. Because the mechanisms \noutlined in Sections 2.1–2.3 tie the predicted effects specifically to \nthe disclosure of a machine origin rather than to the mere presence \nof an explicit source label, each hypothesis below (H1–H3, H8a–\nH8b) makes a paired prediction: a significant effect for the \nAI-generated-label contrast, and no significant effect for the \nhuman-generated-label contrast. If human-generated labels instead \nproduced effects comparable to AI-generated labels, this would \nsuggest that any observed effects reflect source labeling in general \nrather than something specific to AI disclosure. Framed in the \nterms introduced in Section 1.1, H1–H3 test whether the specific \ncontent a label discloses, not merely its presence, is what drives \nthese effects, by comparing two different label contents against the \nsame no-label baseline.\n3.1 First-stage effects of AI disclosure on \ncognitive pathways\nInterface source cues shape how users interpret content (Norman, \n2004; Section 2.1). Building on this logic, AI disclosure is expected to \nreduce perceived authenticity because it disrupts consumers’ default \nassumption of human creative intent behind a product image \n(MacInnis and Price, 1987; Jago, 2017). AI disclosure is also expected \nto reduce esthetic appeal: although generative AI can produce visu-\nally polished images, knowing that an image is machine-generated \nmay suppress rather than enhance esthetic evaluation once the pro-\ncessing-fluency benefit of that polish is weighed against the loss of \nperceived human craftsmanship ( Reber et al., 2004 ; Cetinic and \nShe, 2022 ). Finally, AI disclosure is expected to reduce social pres -\nence, consistent with machine-heuristic accounts in which algo -\nrithms are assumed to lack genuine emotional investment and \nempathy ( Sundar, 2020 ; Mende et al., 2019 ).\nH1: AI-generated disclosure labels (vs. no label) reduce per -\nceived authenticity of the product image; human-generated dis-\nclosure labels (vs. no label) do not.\nH2: AI-generated disclosure labels (vs. no label) reduce per -\nceived esthetic appeal of the product image; human-generated \ndisclosure labels (vs. no label) do not.\nH3: AI-generated disclosure labels (vs. no label) reduce per -\nceived social presence conveyed by the product page; human-\ngenerated disclosure labels (vs. no label) do not.\n3.2 Cognitive pathways to behavioral \noutcomes\nEach of the three cognitive pathways above is expected to \ncarry forward to purchase intention and brand trust. Perceived \nauthenticity signals honesty and genuine commitment, both of \nwhich have been linked to consumer confidence and purchase \nbehavior ( Morhart et al., 2015 ). Esthetic appeal operates through \na processing-fluency mechanism, whereby visually fluent content \ngenerates positive affect that is attributed to the content itself, \nbuilding both engagement and trust ( Reber et al., 2004 ; Dion et \nal., 1972 ). Social presence reduces the psychological distance \nbetween consumer and interface, lowering uncertainty and \nencouraging reciprocity, which is expected to support both pur -\nchase intention and brand trust ( Gefen and Straub, 2004 ; \nHassanein and Head, 2007 ).\nH4a/H4b: Perceived authenticity positively predicts purchase \nintention (H4a) and brand trust (H4b).\nH5a/H5b: Esthetic appeal positively predicts purchase intention \n(H5a) and brand trust (H5b)."}, {"pdf_page": 5, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 05 frontiersin.org\nH6a/H6b: Social presence positively predicts purchase intention \n(H6a) and brand trust (H6b).\n3.3 Moderated mediation: the role of \nproduct type\nBecause utilitarian and hedonic products activate different \nevaluative orientations ( Dhar and Wertenbroch, 2000 ; Section \n2.3), product type is expected to moderate the first-stage effects \nabove, though not necessarily in the same direction for every \npathway. Perceived authenticity may be more threatened by a non-\nhuman source in hedonic contexts, where the original source of \nproduction carries more evaluative weight for consumers \n(Newman and Dhar, 2014 ; Beverland and Farrelly, 2009 ). By con -\ntrast, the negative effect of AI disclosure on esthetic appeal is \nexpected to be more pronounced in utilitarian contexts, where \nsource signals interact with sensory expectations tied to func -\ntional performance rather than emotional creativity ( Hoegg and \nAlba, 2011 ; Longoni and Cian, 2022 ). Similarly, the negative effect \non social presence is expected to be stronger in utilitarian con -\ntexts, where consumers may place particular weight on account -\nability and human responsibility behind functional claims \n(Sundar, 2020 ; Mende et al., 2019 ).\nH7a: Product type moderates the first-stage effect of AI disclo -\nsure (vs. no label) on perceived authenticity, such that the effect \nis stronger in the hedonic context.\nH7b: Product type moderates the first-stage effect of AI disclo -\nsure (vs. no label) on esthetic appeal, such that the negative effect \nis stronger in the utilitarian context.\nH7c: Product type moderates the first-stage effect of AI disclo -\nsure (vs. no label) on social presence, such that the negative \neffect is stronger in the utilitarian context.\n3.4 Direct (transparency/novelty) effects of \nAI disclosure\nBeyond these cognitive pathways, disclosure may independently \nfunction as a transparency signal. Prior work frames AI disclosure as \na “double-edged sword” that can simultaneously carry cognitive costs \nand trust benefits, because acknowledging AI involvement signals \nopenness even when it also changes how the content itself is evaluated \n(Luo et al., 2019 ; Schilke and Reimann, 2025 ). A between-subjects design \nwas chosen to minimize demand effects that could arise from expo-\nsure to multiple conditions.\nData collection was conducted using the Chinese online survey \nplatform SurveyStar. Participants were recruited through social \nmedia platforms such as WeChat and Xiaohongshu, as well as \nthrough the authors’ personal networks, and completed the ques -\ntionnaire online. This convenience and snowball sampling \napproach raises several concerns readers should bear in mind. \nFirst, participants who self-select into an online survey about AI \nand online shopping may already hold stronger opinions about \nAI-generated content than the general population. Second, distrib -\nuting the survey through personal networks may have introduced \nacquaintance bias. Third, the resulting sample is demographically \nskewed (64.9% female, 64.1% aged 18–25, 77.2% with a bachelor’s \ndegree or above, and 71.0% frequent AI users), limiting generaliz -\nability to older, less-educated, or less AI-familiar shoppers. These \nlimitations are discussed further in Section 6.6. Before beginning \nthe survey, participants were informed of the study’s purpose, the \nvoluntary nature of participation, their right to withdraw, and the \nanonymous use of their responses for academic research; electronic \ninformed consent was obtained through voluntary continuation of \nthe questionnaire. Participants then viewed the simulated product \npage and completed the measures for all constructs, followed by \nmanipulation checks and demographic questions. Participants \nwere required to remain on the stimulus page for at least 10 s to \nensure sufficient exposure.\n4.2 E-commerce interface conditions and \nstimuli\nWe selected two product categories to represent different e-com-\nmerce processing orientations, following established criteria for maxi-\nmizing conceptual distance between utilitarian and hedonic domains \n(Dhar and Wertenbroch, 2000; Voss et al., 2003). For the utilitarian \ncondition, we used a portable power bank, a product typically evalu-\nated on functional performance; for the hedonic condition, we used a \nperfume, a product typically evaluated on sensory pleasure and emo-\ntional resonance. Both were presented in the visual format of a typical \ne-commerce product image: a product photo on a plain background, \nstyled consistently with common product-page layouts on platforms \nsuch as Taobao.\nTo isolate the cognitive effects of the disclosure cue itself, all other \npage elements were held constant across conditions: image size, reso-\nlution, font, font size, and color were matched across all six versions. \nThe disclosure label appeared as a text watermark in the upper left  \ncorner of the product image, a placement consistent with common \nregulatory implementation practice that preserves visual prominence \nwithout altering the page layout. Depending on condition, the water-\nmark read “ AI-generated, ” “human-generated, ” or was absent \n(control).\n4.3 Measures\nAll constructs were measured on a 7-point Likert scale \n(1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree), with items adapted from \nvalidated scales. Perceived authenticity (3 items, adapted from Jago, \n2017) captured perceived human creative intent behind the product \nimage. Esthetic appeal (3 items, adapted from Mathwick et al., 2001) \ncaptured perceived visual quality and pleasure. Social presence was \nmeasured with 4 items adapted from Gefen and Straub (2004); the \nfourth item was reverse-worded and was dropped prior to the main \nanalyses after showing a substantially lower item-total correlation than \nthe other three (retaining three items improved scale reliability from \nα = 0.760 to α = 0.887); the three retained items capture perceived \nwarmth, human contact, and psychological closeness. Purchase inten-\ntion (3 items, adapted from Dodds et al., 1991) and brand trust (3 \nitems, adapted from Soh et al., 2009) were measured as the two behav-\nioral outcomes. Perceived risk (3 items, based on Bauer, 1960 ; \nFeatherman and Pavlou, 2003 ; Campbell, 1995) and the uncanny \nvalley effect (3 items, adapted from Ho and MacDorman, 2010) were \nalso measured; as noted above, these two constructs showed no reli-\nable effects and are summarized briefly in Section 5.4 rather than dis-\ncussed in detail. The questionnaire also included an attention-check \nitem to screen inattentive respondents.\n4.4 Participants\nA total of 286 participants completed the survey. Ten question-\nnaires were discarded for failing the attention check, leaving 276 valid \nresponses (97 male, 35.1%; 179 female, 64.9%). Most participants \nheld a bachelor’s degree (77.2%); the largest age group was 18–25 \n(64.1%); 71.0% reported using AI tools multiple times per week. On the \ncognitive-pathway track, AI disclosure labels reduced perceived authen-\nticity, esthetic appeal, and social presence, and the esthetic-appeal and \nsocial-presence pathways were significantly moderated by product type: \nboth the reduction in the mediator and its downstream negative effect \non purchase intention and brand trust were concentrated in the utilitar-\nian product context and were not detectable in the hedonic context. On \nthe direct-effect track, AI disclosure carried an independent positive \neffect on purchase intention, not moderated by product type, that was \nnot explained by the three cognitive mediators and in fact ran opposite \nin sign to their combined negative pull.\nThis opposite-signed pattern is the key nuance that a total-effect-\nonly analysis would miss. It suggests that AI disclosure simultane-\nously (a) erodes perceived authenticity, esthetic quality, and social \nwarmth in the product image, an effect concentrated in utilitarian \ncategories, and (b) carries a separate positive signal, plausibly related \nto perceived transparency, technological currency, or novelty, that \noperates independently of those cognitive costs and is not restricted \nto either product category. Because these two forces partially offset \neach other, the raw, unmediated relationship between AI disclosure \nand purchase behavior looks weak or even negative, even though a \nclear positive channel exists once the cognitive pathways are \naccounted for.\nIn practical terms: picture a shopper scrolling through power \nbank listings on an e-commerce platform. If one listing is water -\nmarked as AI-generated, the product photo reads as slightly less \npolished and less personal, a small but real turn-off that makes \nthat shopper somewhat less inclined to trust the brand or click \nbuy. At the same time, the shopper also picks up a subtle, indepen -\ndent signal of honesty simply because the seller was upfront about \nusing AI, and this alone nudges purchase interest upward a little, \nregardless of how the photo looks. These two reactions pull in \nopposite directions and roughly cancel out, which is why a simple \nbefore-and-after comparison of AI-labeled versus unlabeled list -\nings can look like the label barely matters, even though it is doing \ntwo real and opposite things beneath the surface. For a shopper \nbrowsing perfume rather than power banks, neither reaction \nshows up in a measurable way.\n6.2 A is the effect specific to machine \norigin, or a generic reaction to disclosure?\nAs framed in Section 1.1, the exploratory comparison reported in \nSection 5.4 (Exploratory Questions 1 and 2, Section 3.5) asks whether \nthe specific content of a label matters, not just its presence, and speaks \ndirectly to this question. If shoppers were simply reacting to the pres-\nence of any explicit source label, the AI-generated and human-gener-\nated labels should have produced similar effects. Instead, in the \nutilitarian context, the AI-generated label produced a significantly \nstronger negative effect than the human-generated label on all three \ncognitive mediators, and a significantly stronger positive direct effect \non purchase intention. This pattern favors an account specific to the \ndisclosed machine origin over a more generic explicit-source-label \naccount, and it echoes the foundational role of this same contrast in \nJago (2017) and Luo et al. (2019), on which our theoretical framework \nbuilds (Sections 2.1–2.2). Because this comparison was exploratory \nrather than part of our original confirmatory hypotheses, we treat it \nas suggestive rather than conclusive, and it did not extend to the \nhedonic context or to brand trust, where AI-generated and human-\ngenerated labels produced statistically indistinguishable effects. Future \nconfirmatory work should test this machine-origin-specific account \ndirectly, ideally with a design and sample powered specifically for this \nthree-way comparison.\nTABLE 9 Conditional indirect effects and index of moderated mediation (bootstrapped, 5,000 resamples).\nOutcome Mediator Indirect \neffect \n(utilitarian)\n95% CI Indirect \neffect \n(hedonic)\n95% CI Index of \nmoderated \nmediation\n95% CI\nPurchase intention Perceived \nauthenticity\n–0.081 [–0.213, 0.012] –0.004 [–0.105, 0.096] 0.077 [–0.039, 0.253]\nPurchase intention Esthetic appeal –0.227 [–0.444, –0.061] 0.035 [–0.141, 0.230] 0.262 [0.024, 0.569]\nPurchase intention Social presence –0.464 [–0.799, –0.191] –0.056 [–0.333, 0.223] 0.408 [0.031, 0.866]\nBrand trust Perceived \nauthenticity\n–0.196 [–0.421, –0.009] –0.009 [–0.224, 0.207] 0.187 [–0.089, 0.503]\nBrand trust Esthetic appeal –0.162 [–0.340, –0.031] 0.025 [–0.104, 0.163] 0.186 [0.009, 0.424]\nBrand trust Social presence –0.271 [–0.514, –0.096] –0.033 [–0.203, 0.137] 0.239 [0.019, 0.547]\nBold indicates 95% CI excludes zero. This showed \nthat product type’s moderating role is selective rather than gen -\neral: it applies to the esthetic-appeal and social-presence pathways \nbut not to perceived authenticity, and it does not extend to mod -\nerating the direct (transparency/novelty) effect of AI disclosure. \nThis more granular picture is arguably more actionable for e-com -\nmerce platform design than a single omnibus test would have \nbeen, since it identifies exactly which cognitive pathway differs by \nproduct category: a platform selling power banks has a concrete \nreason to worry about how an AI label affects perceived polish \nand warmth, while a platform selling perfume, based on the pres -\nent data, does not need to worry about this particular path -\nway at all.\n6.5 Theoretical contributions\nFirst, this study identifies a specific statistical signature, inconsis-\ntent mediation (suppression), underlying the long-running debate \nbetween algorithm-aversion and algorithm-appreciation accounts of \nAI disclosure. Rather than concluding that AI disclosure is simply \nharmful or simply beneficial, the present results suggest both effects \ncoexist and partially cancel, which may explain why prior single-\neffect studies have reached inconsistent conclusions depending on \nwhich measure (mediated pathway versus raw total effect) they \nemphasized.\nSecond, this study extends utilitarian–hedonic theorizing on AI \nevaluation (Longoni and Cian, 2022) by showing that the moderating \nrole of product type in e-commerce is pathway-specific rather than \nglobal: esthetic appeal and social presence are moderated, authentic-\nity is not, and the direct transparency/novelty channel is not moder-\nated at all. This qualifies the “word-of-machine effect” account by \nspecifying which cognitive channel it operates through.\nThird, this study complements Shi and Jiang’s (2026) novelty–\nauthenticity trade-off account of AI disclosure in advertising by test-\ning an analogous but distinct three-pathway model in the specific \ncontext of e-commerce product pages, suggesting the broader dual-\ntrack logic (a cognitive-cost channel offset by an independent posi -\ntive signal) may generalize across related but distinct interface \ncontexts.\n6.6 Practical implications for E-commerce \nplatform design\nFor sellers and platforms using AI-generated product imagery, \nthese findings suggest a nuanced approach rather than a blanket rec-\nommendation for or against AI-generated visuals. In utilitarian prod-\nuct categories, AI disclosure carries a real cognitive cost to esthetic \nappeal and perceived social presence, and platforms or sellers may \nwish to pair AI-generated product images with compensating cues, \nsuch as genuine buyer-uploaded photos, video demonstrations, or \nverified reviews, that restore a sense of human presence and visual \ntrust. In hedonic categories, the present data suggest this specific cog-\nnitive cost is less pronounced, though this should not be read as a \nblanket license to use AI-generated imagery without consideration of \ncategory-specific norms. Across both categories, the independent \npositive direct effect of disclosure on purchase intention suggests that \ntransparent labeling itself, done well, need not depress purchase \nbehavior and may even support it, independent of the product \ncategory.\n6.7 Limitations and future work\nThis study has several limitations. First, we tested two product \ncategories, power banks and perfume, chosen to maximize conceptual \ndistance between utilitarian and hedonic orientations; products com-\nbining both attributes (e.g., smartphones, fitness trackers) may show \ndifferent patterns, and future work should test a broader range of \ne-commerce product categories.\nSecond, the disclosure manipulation used a simple text water -\nmark; recognition was imperfect (72.8% correct identification in the \nAI-label condition), which likely attenuated the observed effects and \nshould be considered when interpreting null or marginal findings. \nFuture studies should test alternative label formats and designs \ncommon on e-commerce platforms.\nThird, this study relied on same-source self-reported mea -\nsures collected in a single session; common method variance \ncannot be fully ruled out, though the independent-variable \nmanipulation itself is not subject to this concern. Future work \ncould incorporate behavioral outcomes such as actual click-\nthrough or add-to-cart behavior on a simulated storefront.\nFourth, this study tested a relatively large number of constructs \n(seven total) within a single experiment. This breadth was a deliberate \nchoice intended to provide an initial, exploratory map of the cognitive \npathways activated by AI disclosure on e-commerce product pages, \nrather than to isolate a single mechanism with maximal statistical \npower; we mitigated demand effects and anchoring through respon-\ndent anonymity, randomized item order, and separated measurement \nblocks. We narrowed the main analytic narrative to the three pathways \n(authenticity, esthetic appeal, social presence) that showed reliable \neffects, reporting the two null pathways (perceived risk, uncanny \nvalley) briefly in the text (Section 5.4) rather than removing them \nfrom the study altogether. We agree that future work should test each \npathway in a more targeted, single-mechanism design to further \nstrengthen causal identification and reduce the risk of order or prim-\ning effects across scales.\nFifth, the recruitment method (social media and personal net -\nworks) raises self-selection and acquaintance-bias concerns, and the \nresulting sample is demographically skewed toward young, highly \neducated, AI-familiar respondents, limiting generalizability to older, \nless-educated, or less AI-familiar shoppers. Future studies should use \nstratified or probability sampling across age, education, and \nAI-literacy strata.\nFinally, given cell sizes of 44–48 per condition, the bootstrapped \nconfidence intervals reported here, while informative, are appropri-\nately wide; some effects reported as significant here (particularly those \nwith confidence intervals that narrowly exclude zero) should be \ntreated as an initial estimate to be corroborated by future replications "}, {"pdf_page": 14, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 14 frontiersin.org\nwith larger per-cell samples, and future work could extend the present \n3 × 2 design with a third factor, such as offering tangibility (goods \nversus services), to test the generalizability of the observed utilitarian-\nspecific pattern.\nData availability statement\nThe original contributions presented in the study are included in \nthe article/Supplementary material, further inquiries can be directed \nto the corresponding author.\nEthics statement\nEthical approval was not required for the study involving humans \nin accordance with the local legislation and institutional requirements. \nWritten informed consent to participate in this study was not required \nfrom the participants or the participants’ legal guardians/next of kin \nin accordance with the national legislation and the institutional \nrequirements.\nAuthor contributions\nXY: Conceptualization, Data curation, Methodology, Software, \nValidation, Writing  – original draft, Writing  – review & editing, \nFormal analysis. **Seminar: AI Disclosure in E-Commerce (Yang et al., 2026)**

**Focal Study**
The main investigation is a 3 × 2 between-subjects experiment (p. 1).

**Timed Activity (10 min)**
Analyze the study using the prompts below.
1.  **Design & Setting:** Identify the design and simulated context.
2.  **Sample:** State the recruitment method and final analyzed N.
3.  **Manipulations vs. Measures:** List the manipulated factors and the measured mediators.
4.  **Procedure:** Describe the temporal sequence of the task.
5.  **Key Contrast:** Report the direct effect of AI disclosure on purchase intention (coefficient and p-value).
6.  **Interpretation:** What can the outcome establish about actual behavior? What is a key generalization limitation?
7.  **Nonsignificance:** Why does a non-significant result not prove equivalence?

**Instructor Key**
1.  **Design/Setting:** 3 (disclosure: AI, human, none) × 2 (product: utilitarian, hedonic) between-subjects; simulated e-commerce page (p. 1, 6).
2.  **Sample:** Convenience/snowball sampling via social media; 276 valid responses (p. 6).
3.  **Factors/Measures:** Manipulated: disclosure condition, product type. Measured: authenticity, esthetic appeal, social presence, purchase intention, brand trust (p. 2, 6).
4.  **Procedure:** Random assignment → view stimulus (≥10s) → complete measures → manipulation checks (p. 6).
5.  **Contrast:** Direct effect on purchase intention: b = 0.308, p = 0.010 (p. 10).
6.  **Interpretation:** Purchase intention is a self-reported measure; it does not establish actual purchase behavior (p. 13). Limitation: Sample skewed young/educated/AI-familiar, limiting generalizability (p. 6, 13).
7.  **Nonsignificance:** Nonsignificance indicates insufficient evidence to reject the null, not proof of no effect; wide CIs due to cell sizes (44–48) mean nulls are inconclusive (p. 7).

Explicit source \ndisclosure is not new to e-commerce interfaces, sellers already label \nproducts as handmade, imported, or certified, and the psychological \nlogic of such labels has long been studied as a general phenomenon of \nsource disclosure. What is new, and what motivates the present study, \nis that AI-generated content has recently become one of the most con-\nsequential kinds of content a disclosure label can reveal. We therefore \ntreat AI-generated versus human-generated as two instances of label \ncontent, compared against a shared no-label baseline, and ask how the \npresence of a label, and what that label discloses, shapes shopper \nresponses.\nGenerative artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming \nhow digital product imagery is produced for online retail. AI models \ncan now create highly realistic product images on demand, eliminat-\ning traditional photography costs and production barriers (Dar and \nGul, 2025; Hartmann et al., 2024). This shift is especially visible on \nlarge e-commerce platforms, where sellers increasingly rely on \nAI-generated visuals for product images, the kind a shopper sees while \nbrowsing a listing or reviewing a product before purchase. On plat-\nforms such as Taobao, AI-generated product images have moved from \na novelty to a routine production tool used across many product cat-\negories, from small electronics to cosmetics and fragrance. However, \nwhether shoppers adapt comfortably to this shift remains an open \nquestion, and early evidence suggests they may not do so uniformly.\nGlobal regulators have responded to these developments. Driven \nby concerns about deepfakes and synthetic media, policymakers have \nshifted from voluntary guidelines to enforceable legal requirements. \nFor example, regulations such as the EU’s Artificial Intelligence Act \nand China’s Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI \nServices now require explicit disclosure of AI-generated content \n(Jobin et al., 2019 ; Madiega, 2024 ). In practice, this means that \n“ AI-generated” labels are becoming a standard element of e-commerce \ninterface design, appearing alongside product images on listing and \ndetail pages in much the same way that other source cues (seller \nbadges, certification marks) already do. Unlike most interface cues, \nhowever, an AI-generated label indicates that the visual content was \nnot produced by a human photographer, representing a type of infor-\nmation of a qualitatively different nature that shoppers have little prior \nexperience evaluating (Schilke and Reimann, 2025). AI disclosure is \ntherefore a particularly consequential, currently unfolding instance of \nthe general labeling dynamic introduced above: it lets us ask not only \nwhether a label is present, but whether what the label discloses, a \nmachine origin, changes shopper responses differently than other \nlabel content would.\nThis is at once a design challenge and a regulatory one. Mandatory \ndisclosure labels introduce a new cognitive variable into the product \npage that platform designers cannot ignore. From a human–computer \ninteraction perspective, AI disclosure labels on e-commerce product \npages are not merely regulatory notices; they function as interface-\nlevel source cues that reshape how shoppers attribute agency, authen-\nticity, social presence, and risk to the product images in front of them. \nRather than treating disclosure only as a persuasion problem, we \nconceptualize it as a design variable embedded in human–\nAI-mediated commerce, with implications for transparency design, \nplatform trust, and context-sensitive AI governance.\nExisting research is divided: some work suggests algorithmic dis-\nclosure labels undermine user trust (Oomen et al., 2024), while other \nwork suggests they can increase credibility. This divergence cannot be \nexplained by disclosure condition alone. Prior research shows that \nuser responses to AI vary across utilitarian and hedonic product \ndomains, yet less is known about how AI disclosure labels operate as \ninterface-level source cues specifically within e-commerce product \npages, or which cognitive responses they activate. The gap addressed \nin this study is not the absence of product-context research, but the \nlimited understanding of how AI disclosure cues on e-commerce \nproduct pages shape shoppers’ interpretation of synthetic visual con-\ntent through specific, testable cognitive pathways.\n1.2 Research objectives\nReturning to the labeling dynamic introduced in Section 1.1, and \nbuilding on prior research on algorithm aversion and utilitarian–\nhedonic differences in AI evaluation, this study focuses on a specific \ne-commerce interface problem: how mandatory source disclosure \nlabels on product images function as interface cues and shape pur-\nchase-relevant judgments, using AI-generated content as the focal case \nand human-generated content as a second, comparison case of what \na label can disclose. Rather than asking only whether shoppers prefer \nor reject AI-generated imagery, we examine how disclosure labels, and \nthe content they disclose, reshape shoppers’ cognitive interpretation \nof that imagery and how these interpretations connect to brand trust \nand purchase intention.\nThis study pursues three objectives. First, we examine how source \ndisclosure labels, as interface-level transparency cues on e-commerce \nproduct pages, shape shoppers’ evaluative and behavioral responses \nrelative to a no-label baseline, distinguishing between the general \npresence of a label and the specific content it discloses by comparing \nAI-generated and human-generated label conditions. Second, we \nidentify the cognitive mechanisms through which AI-generated label \ncontent in particular operates, focusing on three mediating variables \nretained as the core analytic focus of this study: perceived authenticity, \nesthetic appeal, and social presence. (Two further constructs, per -\nceived risk and the uncanny valley effect, were also measured and \ntested; because neither showed a reliable first-stage or second-stage \neffect in any product context, neither is carried through the detailed \nresults reported below; a brief summary of their null pattern is given \nin Section 5.4, consistent with the goal of presenting a focused, well-\npowered account of the pathways that matter most.) These three \nretained variables are conceptualized as parallel cognitive responses \nrather than sequential stages in a single causal chain: source-related \njudgment (authenticity), visual evaluation (esthetic appeal), and per-\nceived human presence (social presence). Third, we test whether prod-\nuct context (utilitarian vs. hedonic) moderates the first-stage effect of \nAI disclosure on each of these three pathways, using a conditional \nprocess (moderated-mediation) framework with bootstrapped confi-\ndence intervals, thereby determining the boundary conditions under \nwhich AI disclosure labels function differently across product \ncategories.\nWe employed a 3 × 2 between-subjects experimental design, \nmanipulating disclosure condition and product type. By holding all \nother interface elements of the simulated product page constant, we "}, {"pdf_page": 3, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 03 frontiersin.org\nisolate the cognitive effects of the disclosure cue itself. The findings \naim to inform the design of AI disclosure systems on e-commerce \nplatforms and how shoppers process source information about \nAI-generated product imagery.\n2 Literature review\n2.1 AI disclosure as an interface cue in \nE-commerce\nIn human–computer interaction research, interface cues are \ndesign elements that carry information beyond their surface appear-\nance, shaping how users understand and respond to a system \n(Norman, 2004). A disclosure label is one such cue: whatever it dis-\ncloses, its presence versus absence changes what a shopper knows \nabout the image in front of them. On e-commerce product pages, \nthese labels function as source cues, indicating who, or what, pro -\nduced the image a shopper is evaluating. Regarding AI disclosure \nspecifically, the literature documents two competing patterns.\nAlgorithm aversion refers to the tendency for people to discount \nor reject AI-generated outputs even when their quality is objectively \ncomparable to human-generated outputs. Castelo et al. (2019) suggest \nthis reaction is task-specific, more likely when the task involves sub-\njective judgment, of the kind involved in evaluating a product photo. \nMillet et al. (2023)  attribute this to anthropocentric bias: negative \nreactions to AI signals reflect assumptions about the meaning of the \noutput, not simply an assessment of its quality.\nNot all users react this way. Logg et al. (2019) show that in some \nsituations, people trust an algorithm’s output more than human judg-\nment, especially when objectivity and accuracy are valued, a phenom-\nenon they term “algorithmic appreciation. ” Oomen et al. (2024)  \nfurther show that algorithmic appreciation or aversion largely depends \non the specific evaluative context, which for e-commerce product \nimagery plausibly includes both the product category being shown \nand the shopping task the image supports.\n2.2 Cognitive pathways between disclosure \nand shopper response\nThis study treats three mediating variables, perceived authenticity, \nesthetic appeal, and social presence, as parallel cognitive pathways \nactivated by AI disclosure labels on e-commerce product pages. They \nare not proposed as a sequential process. Perceived authenticity \nreflects a shopper’s attribution of human creative intent and genuine-\nness behind a product image; esthetic appeal reflects visual fluency \nand pleasure in viewing the image; and social presence reflects the \nperceived warmth and human presence conveyed by the product page.\nShoppers typically expect product images to reflect genuine \nhuman creative effort, and this expectation forms the basis of their \nperception of image authenticity (MacInnis and Price, 1987). When a \nlabel indicates that an image originated from a machine, even if the \nimage is visually convincing, it undermines this expectation at a cog-\nnitive level; disclosure reshapes shoppers’ interpretation of the image’s \norigin and dispels the default assumption of a human creator behind \nit (Jago, 2017).\nEsthetic appeal reflects the visual pleasure evoked by a product \nimage during processing (Tractinsky et al., 2000). Processing fluency \ntheory predicts that well-structured stimuli are processed more easily, \ngenerating positive affect that is attributed to the content itself (Reber \net al., 2004). AI-generated images can achieve a high degree of visual \npolish (Cetinic and She, 2022), and in some cases AI labels may rein-\nforce rather than weaken esthetic evaluations by signaling technical \nquality (Verganti et al., 2020).\nSocial presence reflects the warmth and psychological “co-pres-\nence” a shopper experiences when viewing a product page (Short et \nal., 1976; Hassanein and Head, 2007). When shoppers learn that a \nproduct image is AI-generated, they may perceive a lack of genuine \nemotional investment from a human creator. Sundar (2020) links this \nsense of indifference to “machine heuristics, ” the intuitive belief that \nalgorithms inherently lack empathy; Mende et al. (2019) document a \nsimilar anthropomorphic-deprivation effect in service-robot \ninteractions.\nTwo additional constructs, perceived risk and the uncanny valley \neffect, were measured using the same procedures as the three retained \npathways above, motivated by the same broad theoretical logic (that \nAI disclosure could heighten uncertainty about product performance, \nand that machine origin could produce a sense of artificiality even for \nnon-humanoid product images). Neither showed a reliable effect in \nthis study, and this null pattern is discussed further in Section 6.\n2.3 The moderating effect of product \ncontext\nHuman–computer interaction research has consistently shown \nthat the cognitive effect of an interface cue depends on the user’s task \ngoals and the evaluative orientation those goals activate ( Norman, \n2004). Information-source-consistency theory formalizes this: when \nthe source of interface content matches a user’s situational expecta-\ntions, processing is smoother ( Lee and Aaker, 2004 ); a mismatch \nrequires additional cognitive effort to resolve ( Kim and \nDuhachek, 2020).\nUtilitarian and hedonic product contexts activate different pro-\ncessing orientations (Dhar and Wertenbroch, 2000). In utilitarian \ne-commerce categories such as small electronics, AI disclosure may \ncreate competing expectations: it may signal computational precision, \nwhich fits expectations for functional products, but utilitarian prod-\nucts also raise stronger concerns about reliability and real-world per-\nformance, so AI disclosure may trigger caution if shoppers suspect \nthe product image is overly optimized. In hedonic categories such as \nfragrance, shoppers seek emotional resonance and human creative \nexpression, and an AI label may conflict with these expectations \n(Batra and Ahtola, 1991; Longoni and Cian, 2022). Longoni and Cian \n(2022) found that the same AI system is evaluated more favorably in \npractical domains than in hedonic domains, a pattern they term the \n“word-of-machine effect. ”\nA concurrent study by Shi and Jiang (2026) proposes a related but \ndistinct account of AI disclosure effects in advertising, modeling a \ntrade-off between two competing pathways, perceived novelty and \nperceived authenticity, moderated by a shopper’s regulatory focus, \nand also examining product type as a second-stage moderator of this \ntrade-off. The present study differs in structure and scope: rather than \nmodeling a single novelty–authenticity trade-off, we test product type \nas a first-stage moderator of AI disclosure’s effect across three parallel \ncognitive pathways (authenticity, esthetic appeal, social presence) \nspecifically within an e-commerce product-page context, using a \nbootstrapped conditional process framework. These two studies can "}, {"pdf_page": 4, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 04 frontiersin.org\nbe read as complementary accounts of the same underlying phenom-\nenon, approached from different theoretical entry points and inter-\nface contexts (general advertising versus e-commerce product pages).\n2.4 Shopper trust and behavioral \nengagement\nThis study uses two constructs to operationalize behavioral \noutcomes. Brand trust is a form of shopper–platform trust, reflect -\ning confidence in the competence, integrity, and non-deceptive \nintent of the product page’s source ( Mayer et al., 1995 ); even indi -\nrect signals of possible manipulation can weaken this trust \n(Ahluwalia et al., 2000 ). Purchase intention reflects a shopper’s \nwillingness to act on the product page in front of them ( Dodds et \nal., 1991 ); such intentions are sensitive to source and quality cues, \nmaking purchase intention an appropriate behavioral endpoint for \ntesting disclosure effects.\n2.5 A dual-track mechanism of AI \ndisclosure\nAI disclosure labels may influence shoppers through two simul-\ntaneous tracks. The first is a cognitive-penalty pathway: disclosing \nthat a product image is AI-generated may weaken perceived authen-\nticity, reduce social presence, or reduce esthetic appeal, changing how \nshoppers interpret the source and agency behind the image. The \nsecond is a transparency or novelty-signal pathway: disclosure may \nindependently signal openness and honesty, or convey a sense of \ntechnological currency, increasing trust or purchase interest through \na channel that is separate from, and can run in the opposite direction \nto, the cognitive-penalty pathway. As detailed in Section 5, the pres-\nent data are consistent with both tracks operating simultaneously and \nwith partially offsetting signs, a pattern statistically identifiable as \ninconsistent mediation (suppression) once both the indirect and \ndirect effects are estimated within the same model.\n3 Hypotheses\nThe design manipulates disclosure condition at three levels \n(AI-generated label, human-generated label, no label), all esti -\nmated against the same no-label baseline, which serves as the \nsingle reference/control condition throughout. The hypotheses \nbelow treat both label types as manipulated conditions rather than \ntreating one as a passive comparison arm. Because the mechanisms \noutlined in Sections 2.1–2.3 tie the predicted effects specifically to \nthe disclosure of a machine origin rather than to the mere presence \nof an explicit source label, each hypothesis below (H1–H3, H8a–\nH8b) makes a paired prediction: a significant effect for the \nAI-generated-label contrast, and no significant effect for the \nhuman-generated-label contrast. If human-generated labels instead \nproduced effects comparable to AI-generated labels, this would \nsuggest that any observed effects reflect source labeling in general \nrather than something specific to AI disclosure. Framed in the \nterms introduced in Section 1.1, H1–H3 test whether the specific \ncontent a label discloses, not merely its presence, is what drives \nthese effects, by comparing two different label contents against the \nsame no-label baseline.\n3.1 First-stage effects of AI disclosure on \ncognitive pathways\nInterface source cues shape how users interpret content (Norman, \n2004; Section 2.1). Building on this logic, AI disclosure is expected to \nreduce perceived authenticity because it disrupts consumers’ default \nassumption of human creative intent behind a product image \n(MacInnis and Price, 1987; Jago, 2017). AI disclosure is also expected \nto reduce esthetic appeal: although generative AI can produce visu-\nally polished images, knowing that an image is machine-generated \nmay suppress rather than enhance esthetic evaluation once the pro-\ncessing-fluency benefit of that polish is weighed against the loss of \nperceived human craftsmanship ( Reber et al., 2004 ; Cetinic and \nShe, 2022 ). Finally, AI disclosure is expected to reduce social pres -\nence, consistent with machine-heuristic accounts in which algo -\nrithms are assumed to lack genuine emotional investment and \nempathy ( Sundar, 2020 ; Mende et al., 2019 ).\nH1: AI-generated disclosure labels (vs. no label) reduce per -\nceived authenticity of the product image; human-generated dis-\nclosure labels (vs. no label) do not.\nH2: AI-generated disclosure labels (vs. no label) reduce per -\nceived esthetic appeal of the product image; human-generated \ndisclosure labels (vs. no label) do not.\nH3: AI-generated disclosure labels (vs. no label) reduce per -\nceived social presence conveyed by the product page; human-\ngenerated disclosure labels (vs. no label) do not.\n3.2 Cognitive pathways to behavioral \noutcomes\nEach of the three cognitive pathways above is expected to \ncarry forward to purchase intention and brand trust. Perceived \nauthenticity signals honesty and genuine commitment, both of \nwhich have been linked to consumer confidence and purchase \nbehavior ( Morhart et al., 2015 ). Esthetic appeal operates through \na processing-fluency mechanism, whereby visually fluent content \ngenerates positive affect that is attributed to the content itself, \nbuilding both engagement and trust ( Reber et al., 2004 ; Dion et \nal., 1972 ). Social presence reduces the psychological distance \nbetween consumer and interface, lowering uncertainty and \nencouraging reciprocity, which is expected to support both pur -\nchase intention and brand trust ( Gefen and Straub, 2004 ; \nHassanein and Head, 2007 ).\nH4a/H4b: Perceived authenticity positively predicts purchase \nintention (H4a) and brand trust (H4b).\nH5a/H5b: Esthetic appeal positively predicts purchase intention \n(H5a) and brand trust (H5b)."}, {"pdf_page": 5, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 05 frontiersin.org\nH6a/H6b: Social presence positively predicts purchase intention \n(H6a) and brand trust (H6b).\n3.3 Moderated mediation: the role of \nproduct type\nBecause utilitarian and hedonic products activate different \nevaluative orientations ( Dhar and Wertenbroch, 2000 ; Section \n2.3), product type is expected to moderate the first-stage effects \nabove, though not necessarily in the same direction for every \npathway. Perceived authenticity may be more threatened by a non-\nhuman source in hedonic contexts, where the original source of \nproduction carries more evaluative weight for consumers \n(Newman and Dhar, 2014 ; Beverland and Farrelly, 2009 ). By con -\ntrast, the negative effect of AI disclosure on esthetic appeal is \nexpected to be more pronounced in utilitarian contexts, where \nsource signals interact with sensory expectations tied to func -\ntional performance rather than emotional creativity ( Hoegg and \nAlba, 2011 ; Longoni and Cian, 2022 ). Similarly, the negative effect \non social presence is expected to be stronger in utilitarian con -\ntexts, where consumers may place particular weight on account -\nability and human responsibility behind functional claims \n(Sundar, 2020 ; Mende et al., 2019 ).\nH7a: Product type moderates the first-stage effect of AI disclo -\nsure (vs. no label) on perceived authenticity, such that the effect \nis stronger in the hedonic context.\nH7b: Product type moderates the first-stage effect of AI disclo -\nsure (vs. no label) on esthetic appeal, such that the negative effect \nis stronger in the utilitarian context.\nH7c: Product type moderates the first-stage effect of AI disclo -\nsure (vs. no label) on social presence, such that the negative \neffect is stronger in the utilitarian context.\n3.4 Direct (transparency/novelty) effects of \nAI disclosure\nBeyond these cognitive pathways, disclosure may independently \nfunction as a transparency signal. Prior work frames AI disclosure as \na “double-edged sword” that can simultaneously carry cognitive costs \nand trust benefits, because acknowledging AI involvement signals \nopenness even when it also changes how the content itself is evaluated \n(Luo et al., 2019 ; Schilke and Reimann, 2025 ). Building on this \naccount (Section 2.5), AI disclosure labels are expected to carry a posi-\ntive direct effect on purchase intention and brand trust, net of the \ncognitive pathways above.\nH8a: AI disclosure labels have a direct positive effect on pur -\nchase intention, net of the cognitive pathways above; human-\ngenerated disclosure labels do not.\nH8b: AI disclosure labels have a direct positive effect on brand \ntrust, net of the cognitive pathways above; human-generated \ndisclosure labels do not.\nThe research model is shown in Figure 1 (a conditional process \nmodel with three parallel first-stage mediators, product type as a first-\nstage moderator, and a direct path from AI disclosure to each \noutcome).\n3.5 Exploratory analysis: AI-generated \nversus human-generated disclosure\nOur confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H8b, above) already treat \nboth label types as manipulated conditions against the no-label \nbaseline, predicting an effect for the AI-generated-label contrast \nand no effect for the human-generated-label contrast on each path -\nway. These paired predictions do not, however, directly test \nwhether the two label types differ from each other. The founda -\ntional studies motivating our theoretical framework treat this \nFIGURE 1\nProposed conceptual model showing the hypothesized paths tested in this study (H1–H8b), with product type as a first-stage moderator of the \ncognitive pathways."}, {"pdf_page": 6, "text": "Yang et al. 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1860932\nFrontiers in Computer Science 06 frontiersin.org\nAI-versus-human comparison itself as the central manipulation: \nJago (2017)  compares algorithmic work directly against human \nwork across four experiments to establish the authenticity mecha -\nnism we build on (Sections 2.1–2.2), and Luo et al. A between-subjects design \nwas chosen to minimize demand effects that could arise from expo-\nsure to multiple conditions.\nData collection was conducted using the Chinese online survey \nplatform SurveyStar. Participants were recruited through social \nmedia platforms such as WeChat and Xiaohongshu, as well as \nthrough the authors’ personal networks, and completed the ques -\ntionnaire online. This convenience and snowball sampling \napproach raises several concerns readers should bear in mind. \nFirst, participants who self-select into an online survey about AI \nand online shopping may already hold stronger opinions about \nAI-generated content than the general population. Second, distrib -\nuting the survey through personal networks may have introduced \nacquaintance bias. Third, the resulting sample is demographically \nskewed (64.9% female, 64.1% aged 18–25, 77.2% with a bachelor’s \ndegree or above, and 71.0% frequent AI users), limiting generaliz -\nability to older, less-educated, or less AI-familiar shoppers. These \nlimitations are discussed further in Section 6.6. Before beginning \nthe survey, participants were informed of the study’s purpose, the \nvoluntary nature of participation, their right to withdraw, and the \nanonymous use of their responses for academic research; electronic \ninformed consent was obtained through voluntary continuation of \nthe questionnaire. Participants then viewed the simulated product \npage and completed the measures for all constructs, followed by \nmanipulation checks and demographic questions. Participants \nwere required to remain on the stimulus page for at least 10 s to \nensure sufficient exposure.\n4.2 E-commerce interface conditions and \nstimuli\nWe selected two product categories to represent different e-com-\nmerce processing orientations, following established criteria for maxi-\nmizing conceptual distance between utilitarian and hedonic domains \n(Dhar and Wertenbroch, 2000; Voss et al., 2003). For the utilitarian \ncondition, we used a portable power bank, a product typically evalu-\nated on functional performance; for the hedonic condition, we used a \nperfume, a product typically evaluated on sensory pleasure and emo-\ntional resonance. Both were presented in the visual format of a typical \ne-commerce product image: a product photo on a plain background, \nstyled consistently with common product-page layouts on platforms \nsuch as Taobao.\nTo isolate the cognitive effects of the disclosure cue itself, all other \npage elements were held constant across conditions: image size, reso-\nlution, font, font size, and color were matched across all six versions. \nThe disclosure label appeared as a text watermark in the upper left  \ncorner of the product image, a placement consistent with common \nregulatory implementation practice that preserves visual prominence \nwithout altering the page layout. Depending on condition, the water-\nmark read “ AI-generated, ” “human-generated, ” or was absent \n(control).\n4.3 Measures\nAll constructs were measured on a 7-point Likert scale \n(1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree), with items adapted from \nvalidated scales. Perceived authenticity (3 items, adapted from Jago, \n2017) captured perceived human creative intent behind the product \nimage. Esthetic appeal (3 items, adapted from Mathwick et al., 2001) \ncaptured perceived visual quality and pleasure. Social presence was \nmeasured with 4 items adapted from Gefen and Straub (2004); the \nfourth item was reverse-worded and was dropped prior to the main \nanalyses after showing a substantially lower item-total correlation than \nthe other three (retaining three items improved scale reliability from \nα = 0.760 to α = 0.887); the three retained items capture perceived \nwarmth, human contact, and psychological closeness. Purchase inten-\ntion (3 items, adapted from Dodds et al., 1991) and brand trust (3 \nitems, adapted from Soh et al., 2009) were measured as the two behav-\nioral outcomes. Perceived risk (3 items, based on Bauer, 1960 ; \nFeatherman and Pavlou, 2003 ; Campbell, 1995) and the uncanny \nvalley effect (3 items, adapted from Ho and MacDorman, 2010) were \nalso measured; as noted above, these two constructs showed no reli-\nable effects and are summarized briefly in Section 5.4 rather than dis-\ncussed in detail. The questionnaire also included an attention-check \nitem to screen inattentive respondents.\n4.4 Participants\nA total of 286 participants completed the survey. Ten question-\nnaires were discarded for failing the attention check, leaving 276 valid \nresponses (97 male, 35.1%; 179 female, 64.9%). Most participants \nheld a bachelor’s degree (77.2%); the largest age group was 18–25 \n(64.1%); 71.0% reported using AI tools multiple times per week. On the \ncognitive-pathway track, AI disclosure labels reduced perceived authen-\nticity, esthetic appeal, and social presence, and the esthetic-appeal and \nsocial-presence pathways were significantly moderated by product type: \nboth the reduction in the mediator and its downstream negative effect \non purchase intention and brand trust were concentrated in the utilitar-\nian product context and were not detectable in the hedonic context. On \nthe direct-effect track, AI disclosure carried an independent positive \neffect on purchase intention, not moderated by product type, that was \nnot explained by the three cognitive mediators and in fact ran opposite \nin sign to their combined negative pull.\nThis opposite-signed pattern is the key nuance that a total-effect-\nonly analysis would miss. It suggests that AI disclosure simultane-\nously (a) erodes perceived authenticity, esthetic quality, and social \nwarmth in the product image, an effect concentrated in utilitarian \ncategories, and (b) carries a separate positive signal, plausibly related \nto perceived transparency, technological currency, or novelty, that \noperates independently of those cognitive costs and is not restricted \nto either product category. Because these two forces partially offset \neach other, the raw, unmediated relationship between AI disclosure \nand purchase behavior looks weak or even negative, even though a \nclear positive channel exists once the cognitive pathways are \naccounted for.\nIn practical terms: picture a shopper scrolling through power \nbank listings on an e-commerce platform. If one listing is water -\nmarked as AI-generated, the product photo reads as slightly less \npolished and less personal, a small but real turn-off that makes \nthat shopper somewhat less inclined to trust the brand or click \nbuy. At the same time, the shopper also picks up a subtle, indepen -\ndent signal of honesty simply because the seller was upfront about \nusing AI, and this alone nudges purchase interest upward a little, \nregardless of how the photo looks. These two reactions pull in \nopposite directions and roughly cancel out, which is why a simple \nbefore-and-after comparison of AI-labeled versus unlabeled list -\nings can look like the label barely matters, even though it is doing \ntwo real and opposite things beneath the surface. For a shopper \nbrowsing perfume rather than power banks, neither reaction \nshows up in a measurable way.\n6.2 A is the effect specific to machine \norigin, or a generic reaction to disclosure?\nAs framed in Section 1.1, the exploratory comparison reported in \nSection 5.4 (Exploratory Questions 1 and 2, Section 3.5) asks whether \nthe specific content of a label matters, not just its presence, and speaks \ndirectly to this question. If shoppers were simply reacting to the pres-\nence of any explicit source label, the AI-generated and human-gener-\nated labels should have produced similar effects. Instead, in the \nutilitarian context, the AI-generated label produced a significantly \nstronger negative effect than the human-generated label on all three \ncognitive mediators, and a significantly stronger positive direct effect \non purchase intention. This pattern favors an account specific to the \ndisclosed machine origin over a more generic explicit-source-label \naccount, and it echoes the foundational role of this same contrast in \nJago (2017) and Luo et al. (2019), on which our theoretical framework \nbuilds (Sections 2.1–2.2). Because this comparison was exploratory \nrather than part of our original confirmatory hypotheses, we treat it \nas suggestive rather than conclusive, and it did not extend to the \nhedonic context or to brand trust, where AI-generated and human-\ngenerated labels produced statistically indistinguishable effects. Future \nconfirmatory work should test this machine-origin-specific account \ndirectly, ideally with a design and sample powered specifically for this \nthree-way comparison.\nTABLE 9 Conditional indirect effects and index of moderated mediation (bootstrapped, 5,000 resamples).\nOutcome Mediator Indirect \neffect \n(utilitarian)\n95% CI Indirect \neffect \n(hedonic)\n95% CI Index of \nmoderated \nmediation\n95% CI\nPurchase intention Perceived \nauthenticity\n–0.081 [–0.213, 0.012] –0.004 [–0.105, 0.096] 0.077 [–0.039, 0.253]\nPurchase intention Esthetic appeal –0.227 [–0.444, –0.061] 0.035 [–0.141, 0.230] 0.262 [0.024, 0.569]\nPurchase intention Social presence –0.464 [–0.799, –0.191] –0.056 [–0.333, 0.223] 0.408 [0.031, 0.866]\nBrand trust Perceived \nauthenticity\n–0.196 [–0.421, –0.009] –0.009 [–0.224, 0.207] 0.187 [–0.089, 0.503]\nBrand trust Esthetic appeal –0.162 [–0.340, –0.031] 0.025 [–0.104, 0.163] 0.186 [0.009, 0.424]\nBrand trust Social presence –0.271 [–0.514, –0.096] –0.033 [–0.203, 0.137] 0.239 [0.019, 0.547]\nBold indicates 95% CI excludes zero.
